(a) Both models give the atom the same overall size, of order \(10^{-10}\,\text{m}\); they differ in how the charge and mass are arranged inside that volume, not in the size of the atom itself.
(b) In Thomson's model the positive charge is spread through the whole atom, so an electron embedded in it sits where the net force on it is zero and is in stable equilibrium. In Rutherford's model the electron orbits a point nucleus and is always pulled towards it, so it always experiences a net (centripetal) force.
(c) In Rutherford's model the orbiting electron is continuously accelerated; by classical electromagnetic theory an accelerated charge radiates, so the electron would steadily lose energy and spiral into the nucleus.
(d) Thomson's model spreads the positive charge, and therefore almost all the mass, uniformly over the atom, giving a nearly continuous mass distribution; Rutherford's model concentrates that mass in a tiny nucleus, which is highly non-uniform.
(e) An electron is about \(1836\) times lighter than a proton, so in either picture the positively charged part carries almost the whole mass of the atom.

A hydrogen nucleus is a single proton, so it differs from a gold nucleus in two ways that both matter: its charge number is \(Z = 1\) instead of \(Z = 79\), and its mass is about one quarter of the mass of an \(\alpha\)-particle instead of about \(50\) times greater.

The Coulomb repulsion is proportional to \(Z\), so at a given separation the deflecting force is about \(79\) times smaller, and the distance of closest approach \(d = 2Ze^{2}/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 K)\) is \(79\) times smaller than for gold.

More decisively, the target is now lighter than the projectile. In an elastic collision a heavier projectile cannot be turned through more than
\(\theta_{\max} = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{m_{\text{target}}}{m_{\text{projectile}}}\right) = \sin^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \approx 14.5^\circ\)
whatever the impact parameter, because the light proton simply recoils and carries momentum away. Large-angle and backward scattering are therefore impossible in principle, not merely rare.

Essentially every \(\alpha\)-particle would pass through the sheet with only a small deflection and none would be scattered backwards, so the experiment would give no evidence at all for a small, massive, positively charged nucleus.

The emitted photon carries away the whole separation between the two levels, so \(h\nu = \Delta E\).
\(\Delta E = 2.3\,\text{eV} = 2.3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 3.68 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)
\(\nu = \dfrac{\Delta E}{h} = \dfrac{3.68 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}}{6.62 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}\)
\(\nu = 5.6 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\)

For an electron held to the proton by the Coulomb force,
\(K = \dfrac{e^{2}}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\) and \(U = -\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\),
so \(U = -2K\) and the total energy is \(E = K + U = -K\).
Hence \(K = -E\) and \(U = 2E\).
With \(E = -13.6\,\text{eV}\):
\(K = 13.6\,\text{eV}\)
\(U = -27.2\,\text{eV}\)

The hydrogen levels are \(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\,\text{eV}\), so
\(E_1 = -13.6\,\text{eV}\) and \(E_4 = -\dfrac{13.6}{16} = -0.85\,\text{eV}\).
The photon must supply the whole gap:
\(\Delta E = E_4 - E_1 = -0.85 - (-13.6) = 12.75\,\text{eV} = 12.75 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J} = 2.04 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\)
\(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{(6.62 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}{2.04 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}} = 9.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{m}\)
\(\nu = \dfrac{\Delta E}{h} = \dfrac{2.04 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}}{6.62 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}} = 3.1 \times 10^{15}\,\text{Hz}\)
Wavelength \(= 9.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{m}\) (about \(97\,\text{nm}\)); frequency \(= 3.1 \times 10^{15}\,\text{Hz}\).

(a) Combining Bohr's quantisation \(m v_n r_n = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\) with the orbit radius \(r_n = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m e^{2}}\) gives
\(v_n = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2\varepsilon_0 n h}\), so \(v_n \propto \dfrac{1}{n}\).
\(v_1 = \dfrac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C})^{2}}{2(8.854 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{F m}^{-1})(6.62 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})} = 2.18 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
\(v_2 = \dfrac{v_1}{2} = 1.09 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
\(v_3 = \dfrac{v_1}{3} = 7.27 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(b) The orbital period is \(T_n = \dfrac{2\pi r_n}{v_n}\) with \(r_n = n^{2}(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m})\). Since \(r_n \propto n^{2}\) and \(v_n \propto 1/n\), \(T_n \propto n^{3}\).
\(T_1 = \dfrac{2\pi(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m})}{2.18 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}} = 1.52 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{s}\)
\(T_2 = 8T_1 = 1.22 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{s}\)
\(T_3 = 27T_1 = 4.12 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{s}\)

(a) \(v_1 = 2.18 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(v_2 = 1.09 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(v_3 = 7.27 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
(b) \(T_1 = 1.52 \times 10^{-16}\,\text{s}\), \(T_2 = 1.22 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{s}\), \(T_3 = 4.12 \times 10^{-15}\,\text{s}\)

In Bohr's model the orbit radii scale as the square of the principal quantum number, \(r_n = n^{2}a_0\), where \(a_0 = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\) is the innermost (\(n = 1\)) radius.
\(r_2 = 2^{2}a_0 = 4 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m} = 2.12 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\)
\(r_3 = 3^{2}a_0 = 9 \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m} = 4.77 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\)
\(r_2 = 2.12 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\), \(r_3 = 4.77 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{m}\)

At room temperature the atoms are in the ground state, so the beam must supply the full excitation energy from \(n = 1\). Using \(E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}\,\text{eV}\):
\(E_2 - E_1 = 10.2\,\text{eV}\), \(E_3 - E_1 = 12.09\,\text{eV}\), \(E_4 - E_1 = 12.75\,\text{eV}\)
An electron of \(12.5\,\text{eV}\) can excite an atom to \(n = 3\) but not to \(n = 4\), so \(n = 3\) is the highest level reached.
De-excitation from \(n = 3\) can follow three routes, and \(\lambda = hc/\Delta E\) gives
\(3 \to 1\): \(\Delta E = 12.09\,\text{eV}\), \(\lambda = 1.03 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 102.7\,\text{nm}\)
\(2 \to 1\): \(\Delta E = 10.2\,\text{eV}\), \(\lambda = 1.22 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 121.7\,\text{nm}\)
\(3 \to 2\): \(\Delta E = 1.89\,\text{eV}\), \(\lambda = 6.57 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m} = 657\,\text{nm}\)
The transitions ending on \(n = 1\) belong to the Lyman series and the one ending on \(n = 2\) to the Balmer series.
Two series are emitted: the Lyman series, at \(102.7\,\text{nm}\) and \(121.7\,\text{nm}\), and the Balmer series, at \(657\,\text{nm}\).

Applying Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum to the earth-sun system, \(L = m v r = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), so
\(n = \dfrac{2\pi m v r}{h}\)
\(n = \dfrac{2\pi(6.0 \times 10^{24}\,\text{kg})(3 \times 10^{4}\,\text{m s}^{-1})(1.5 \times 10^{11}\,\text{m})}{6.62 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}\)
\(n = 2.6 \times 10^{74}\)
The quantum number is so enormous that neighbouring levels are indistinguishably close and the orbit appears perfectly continuous, which is the classical limit of the Bohr model.
\(n \approx 2.6 \times 10^{74}\)
